newsitem.title: UK: Lockheed links up with Intersputnik.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed links up with Intersputnik.

text.p: U.S. defence and aerospace giant Lockheed Martin Corp strengthened its Russian space interests on Monday by confirming a joint venture with Intersputnik, the former Soviet space agency, to provide worldwide satellite communications.

Lockheed, which expects the booming $3-4 billion global market in fixed satellite services to show 15 percent annual compound growth, will take a large but unspecified majority in its third space deal with Russia.

However industry sources said the U.S. heavyweight's holding would be around 70 percent in its latest venture -- Lockheed Martin Intersputnik Ltd (LMI) -- which is expected to generate annual revenues of $300-$500 million by 2001.

Headquartered in London and with a marketing office in Moscow, LMI plans to launch its first geostationary satellite in the fourth quarter of 1998 and, in the first of three phases, three others by 2000.

If growth projections ring true and LMI launches 15 satellites into orbit and leases space on them for voice, video, data and fax services, annual revenues could surge to $1.5 billion in five to 10 years, Lockheed's vice president, strategic development Brian Dailey said.

"We are extremely pleased to have Intersputnik as partners in such an exciting venture," said Mel Brashears, president and chief operating officer of Lockheed's space and strategic missile sector business after the deal was unveiled in London.
"The combination of our two organisations results in a new and highly competitive global satellite services supplier," he added.

Intersputnik's deputy director general Istvan Kovach said the organisation, which operates a key satellite communication system and provides international, regional and domestic communications, had been in talks with 14 organisations over the last two-and-a-half years before sealing an agreement with Lockheed.

Lockheed, which has successfully launched 650 satellites and developed 100 launch vehicles, declined to comment on when the venture would be profitable or how much it was investing because of a highly competitive nature of the satellite telecommunications business.

Initially, the new satellite company will provide communications to customers in eastern Europe, South Asia, Africa and the Commonwealth of Independent States before expanding to a full global service.
Broadcast and telecommunications services will also be boosted to include direct-to-home video and audio and mobile services to customers worldwide.

Gennady Kudryavstev, director general of Intersputnik International Organisation of Space Communications -- which was established over 25 years ago during the Cold War days and has 22 member countries -- said the new company would provide cutting edge solutions to customers' communications needs.
"We will pursue excellence and growth through co-operation, continuous improvement and innovation," he said.
Lockheed Martin, based in Bethesda, Maryland, designs, manufactures and supports advanced technology systems for domestic and international military, classified, civil and commercial markets.
